implementation_notes: Spring Integration ships the pattern as an interface: MessageStore.addMessage/getMessage/removeMessage (plus getMessageMetadata for querying without deserialising) with JdbcMessageStore backed by the packaged int_message/int_group schema, MongoDbMessageStore, RedisMessageStore and a SimpleMessageStore for tests; regions separate independent audit streams. Wire the copy off the main path with a Wire Tap or an outbound channel interceptor whose handler calls store.addMessage, and route the tap's failures to a counted error channel, because a tap that throws would push store availability into the delivery path. Reporting reads the store directly (or the owning database), and retention is a scheduled job calling removeMessage / expiring groups, or plain SQL when the application owns the schema. Choose this variant when the application already runs Spring Integration; the classic hand-written structure remains the better choice when one audit table is the only reason to add the dependency.
pitfalls: A Wire Tap handler that throws (or an unconfigured error channel) can propagate into the main flow; route tap failures to a counted error channel so the copy stays best-effort.
JdbcMessageStore tables grow without bound: retention or group expiry must be scheduled, or the audit store quietly becomes the largest table in the database.
getMessage deserialises stored payloads with the application's converters; a later payload-class change makes old rows unreadable unless serialisation is versioned or stored as explicit JSON.
Sharing one region between unrelated flows mixes records and their retention rules; separate regions (or stores) keep each stream's policy and access separable.

variants.name: Hand-written JDBC store with batched inserts
variants.implementation_notes: Without a framework the store is a small repository: a DataSource, one prepared INSERT executed in batches inside a single transaction (setAutoCommit(false), addBatch, executeBatch, commit), so durability costs one fsync per batch instead of one per message, plus an index on the report columns (correlation id, channel, recorded_at). The tap is a bounded BlockingQueue drained by one writer thread, which is what keeps the delivery path from touching the connection. Retention is a scheduled DELETE by timestamp, or a partitioned table where the database offers partitioning. Choose this variant when the application already owns its schema and the only reason to add a framework would be this one table; choose the Spring Integration variant when the flow is already built from channels and endpoints.
pitfalls: With auto-commit left on, every message costs its own transaction and fsync; batching plus an explicit commit is what makes the store affordable at message rates.

JDBC objects are not thread-safe: sharing a Connection or PreparedStatement between the delivery thread and the writer corrupts batches - hand records to a single writer, not the connection to everyone.
Without an index on the reporting columns the audit queries scan a growing table; the index is part of the pattern, not an optimisation to add later.
Unbounded retention turns the table into the database's largest object; a scheduled DELETE by timestamp (or partitioning) belongs in the same repository as the insert.
